+\begin{definition}[Directly indexed sub-line laws]
+	\label{def:direct-subline-law}
+	\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.SubLineWitness}
+	\leanok
+	\uses{def:ith-restricted-line, def:line-representative, def:combine-map}
+	Put $n=2m+2$. The directly indexed extended line-point law samples
+	$i\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $u,v\in\F_q^n$ independently and uniformly,
+	and chooses the axis or diagonal kind with equal probabilities.
+	For the axis kind set $w=e_i$; for the diagonal kind set $w_j=0$ for
+	$j<i$ and $w_j=v_j$ for $j\ge i$. The line has base $L_w^{\mathrm{lnf}}(u)$
+	and direction $w$, retaining its kind and coordinate index; the sampled
+	point is $u$. Zero diagonal directions are included.
+
+	A directly indexed sub-line law $D_{\mathrm{dir}}$ is a probability law
+	on triples $(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z)$ with the following properties.
+	Its extended-line marginal is the line marginal just defined.
+	Every supported triple admits affine maps $t\mapsto a_W+b_Wt$ such that
+	\[
+		\pi_W(\ell(t))=\ell_W(a_W+b_Wt),\qquad W\in\{X,Z\},
+	\]
+	where $\ell(t)$ denotes base plus parameter times direction and the
+	field identifications are understood. Thus each extended point projects
+	onto its two source lines, with affine scalar coordinates $\alpha(t)$
+	and $\beta(t)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:combine-map}. An axis-parallel
+	extended line has axis-parallel source lines.
+
+	Finally there is one probability law on
+	$(\mathrm v,i,j)\in\{\mathrm{ALine},\mathrm{DLine}\}
+	\times\{0,\dots,m-1\}^2$ with the following two mixture properties.
+	Sample a triple from $D_{\mathrm{dir}}$ and an independent uniform
+	parameter $t$ on $\ell$. The law of $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,\pi_X(\ell(t)))$
+	is the mixture obtained by sampling $(\ell_X,x)$ from
+	$D_{\mathrm v,i}$ and independently $\ell_Z$ from the line marginal of
+	$D_{\mathrm v,j}$, and retaining $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,x)$.
+	The law of $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,\pi_Z(\ell(t)))$ is the mixture obtained
+	by retaining $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,z)$ from the corresponding independent
+	samples of $\ell_X$ and $(\ell_Z,z)$. These are separate one-point
+	marginal identities, with the same mixture weights; they impose no
+	joint conditional independence of the two projected points.
+	Identification with the source law $D$ is a separate obligation;
+	see \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}.
+\end{definition}

+	\leanok
+	\uses{def:admissible}
+	There is no function $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
+	$0\leq f(x,y)\leq C(x^r+y^s)$ on the closed nonnegative quadrant,
+	for constants $C\geq 1$ and
+	$r,s>0$, which satisfies
+	\[
+		\min\{1,m\eps^{1/4}\}\leq f(m^2\eps,md/q)
+	\]
+	for every admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every $\eps\geq0$.
+	This is a scalar obstruction to the first proof route in
+	Remark~\ref{rem:qld-4-13-source-defects}, not a counterexample to
+	Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}.
+\end{lemma}
+\begin{proof}
+	\leanok
+	Set $m_n=2^{2n+1}$, $d_n=1$, $q_n=m_n^3$, and $\eps_n=m_n^{-4}$.
+	These parameters are admissible: $q_n=2^{6n+3}$ has odd exponent and
+	$m_n\mid q_n$. Both arguments of $f$ equal $m_n^{-2}$, so the assumed
+	polynomial upper bound tends to zero. But
+	$\min\{1,m_n\eps_n^{1/4}\}=1$ for every $n$, a contradiction.
+\end{proof}

 /-- A pair of source points and the two scalar coefficients used by the
 extended point measurement. -/
 abbrev ExtendedPointQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) ×
     (PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P)

 /-- Coarse-grain a joint point measurement by `(a,b) |-> alpha*a + beta*b`
 on the selected player side.  This is the concrete measurement of
 `lem:qld-4-12`, paper lines 993--1011. -/
 noncomputable def extendedQ {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δ : ℝ}
     {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δ)
     (side : PlayerSide) (x z : Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)
     (alpha beta : PauliScalar P) :
     Measurement (PauliScalar P) (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   (points.Q side x z).postprocess fun ab => alpha * ab.1 + beta * ab.2
 
+/-- The first postprocessed joint-point effect is its X marginal sum.
+This formalization-only identity is the definition preceding
+`eq:qld-qxz-close-to-point`, paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:917-932`. -/
+theorem postprocess_fst_effect {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δQ : ℝ}
+    {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δQ)
+    (side : PlayerSide) (x z : Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
+    ((points.Q side x z).postprocess Prod.fst).effect a =
+      ∑ b, (points.Q side x z).effect (a, b) := by
+  classical
+  change (∑ pair ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun pair => pair.1 = a),
+    (points.Q side x z).effect pair) = _
+  simp only [Finset.sum_filter, Fintype.sum_prod_type]
+  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
+  simp
+
+/-- The second postprocessed joint-point effect is its Z marginal sum.
+This formalization-only identity is `eq:qld-qxz-close-to-point-2`, paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:933-935`. -/
+theorem postprocess_snd_effect {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δQ : ℝ}
+    {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δQ)
+    (side : PlayerSide) (x z : Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) (b : PauliScalar P) :
+    ((points.Q side x z).postprocess Prod.snd).effect b =
+      ∑ a, (points.Q side x z).effect (a, b) := by
+  classical
+  change (∑ pair ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun pair => pair.2 = b),
+    (points.Q side x z).effect pair) = _
+  simp [Finset.sum_filter, Fintype.sum_prod_type]
+
 end CombinedPointsWitness
 
 /-- Construction of the projective joint point measurements of
 `lem:qld-4-10`, paper lines 689--709.  The witness retains both ordered
 products and all four directed heterogeneous placement comparisons.
 
 The construction works on the original expanded local spaces: the sandwich
 POVM `M^Z_b M^X_a M^Z_b`, formed directly with outcomes in `F_q × F_q`, is
 close to the ordered product by the field-valued commutation estimate
 (`expPoint_comm`), self-consistent between opposite placements
 (`sandwich_offDiagonal_le_sandwichDefectBound`), and is made projective for
 each point pair by the orthonormalization lemma
 (`exists_projective_close_sandwich`); the three consistency conclusions follow
 by the triangle inequality (`chain_bounds`).  The source's route through the
 binary refinements and the quantum linearity theorem is not used, because
 that route needs zero-state padding of the strategy, which is not part of the
 setting; see `rem:linearity-import` and
 `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_combined-points-direct.tex`.  The error is
 `K ε^{1/8}` for a universal constant `K`. -/
 theorem exists_combinedPointsWitness :
     ∃ deltaQ : ℝ -> ℝ, IsPolyErr deltaQ ∧
       ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) (ε : ℝ) (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε),
         Nonempty (CombinedPointsWitness S (deltaQ ε)) := by
   obtain ⟨C₀, hC₀, h₀⟩ := ProjectiveSetting.avg_sandwichDefectBound_le
   obtain ⟨C₁, hC₁, h₁⟩ := ProjectiveSetting.sandwichPoint_ordered_dist_le
   obtain ⟨C₂, hC₂, h₂⟩ := ProjectiveSetting.expPoint_comm
   obtain ⟨C₃, hC₃, h₃⟩ := ProjectiveSetting.ordered_cross_dist_le
   -- the universal constant of the final error `K ε^{1/8}`
   set K : ℝ := 12 * (440 * (2 * C₀)) + 20 * C₁ + 16 * C₃ + 4 * C₂ with hK
   have hK4 : (4 : ℝ) ≤ K := by rw [hK]; nlinarith

    70	    rw [Finset.mul_sum, Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
    71	    exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun a _ => by ring
    72	  have hμ : (∑ a ∈ μ.support ∪ ν.support, μ.weight a * f a) =
    73	      ∑ a ∈ μ.support, μ.weight a * f a := by
    74	    refine (Finset.sum_subset Finset.subset_union_left ?_).symm
    75	    intro a _ ha

    86	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary: an average against a product law is the

    89	theorem avgOver_prod {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]

    91	    avgOver (Distribution.prod μ ν) f =
    92	      avgOver μ (fun a => avgOver ν (fun b => f (a, b))) := by
    93	  classical
    94	  unfold avgOver

   107	    (ν : ι → Distribution β) (f : β → ℝ) (hf : ∀ b, 0 ≤ f b) (i : ι) :

   109	      avgOver (Distribution.bind (uniformDistribution ι) ν) f := by
   110	  classical
   111	  rw [avgOver_bind]

   113	      0 ≤ (uniformDistribution ι).weight j * avgOver (ν j) f := fun j _ =>
   114	    mul_nonneg ((uniformDistribution ι).nonnegative j) (avgOver_nonneg _ _ hf)
   115	  have hsingle := Finset.single_le_sum
   116	    (f := fun j => (uniformDistribution ι).weight j * avgOver (ν j) f)
   117	    hterm (Finset.mem_univ i)

   121	/-! ## Inflation of a restricted line-point average -/
   122	
   123	/-- Restricting a nonnegative line-point average to one kind and one coordinate
   124	index inflates it by at most `2 m`.  This is the pointwise form of item 1 of
   125	blueprint `lem:restricted-line-mixture-bounds`, paper
   126	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1052-1056`. -/
   127	theorem avgOver_restrictedLinePointDist_le {P : AdmissibleParams}
   128	    (f : (LineDesc P.toLdParams × (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)) → ℝ)
   129	    (hf : ∀ sample, 0 ≤ f sample) (kind : LineKind) (i : Fin P.m) :
   130	    avgOver (restrictedLinePointDist P kind i) f ≤
   131	      2 * (P.m : ℝ) * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f := by
   132	  classical
   133	  haveI : Nonempty (Fin P.m) :=
   134	    Fin.pos_iff_nonempty.mp (lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.one_le_m)
   135	  have hm : (0 : ℝ) < (P.m : ℝ) := by
   136	    exact_mod_cast lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.one_le_m
   137	  have hAnonneg : 0 ≤ avgOver (aLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f :=
   138	    avgOver_nonneg _ _ hf
   139	  have hDnonneg : 0 ≤ avgOver (dLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f :=
   140	    avgOver_nonneg _ _ hf
   141	  have hmixture : avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f =
   142	      1 / 2 * avgOver (aLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f +
   143	        (1 - 1 / 2) * avgOver (dLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f :=
   144	    avgOver_mix _ _ _ _ _ f
   145	  -- Each kind is bounded by twice the full line-point average.
   146	  have hsum : 2 * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f =
   147	      avgOver (aLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f +
   148	        avgOver (dLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f := by
   149	    rw [hmixture]
   150	    ring
   151	  have hAle : avgOver (aLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f ≤
   152	      2 * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f := by
   153	    rw [hsum]
   154	    exact le_add_of_nonneg_right hDnonneg
   155	  have hDle : avgOver (dLinePointDist P.toLdParams) f ≤
   156	      2 * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f := by
   157	    rw [hsum]
   158	    exact le_add_of_nonneg_left hAnonneg
   159	  -- The coordinate index contributes a further factor `m`.
   160	  have hcomponent : ∀ (ν : Fin P.m → Distribution (LineDesc P.toLdParams ×
   161	      (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))) (μ : Distribution (LineDesc P.toLdParams ×
   162	      (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))),
   163	      μ = Distribution.bind (uniformDistribution (Fin P.m)) ν →
   164	      avgOver μ f ≤ 2 * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f →
   165	      avgOver (ν i) f ≤ 2 * (P.m : ℝ) * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f := by
   166	    intro ν μ hbind hle
   167	    have hcomp := avgOver_bind_uniform_component_le ν f hf i
   168	    rw [Fintype.card_fin, ← hbind] at hcomp
   169	    have hstep : avgOver (ν i) f ≤ (P.m : ℝ) * avgOver μ f := by
   170	      rw [div_mul_eq_mul_div, one_mul, div_le_iff₀ hm] at hcomp
   171	      rw [mul_comm]
   172	      exact hcomp
   173	    calc avgOver (ν i) f ≤ (P.m : ℝ) * avgOver μ f := hstep
   174	      _ ≤ (P.m : ℝ) * (2 * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f) := by
   175	          exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hle (le_of_lt hm)
   176	      _ = 2 * (P.m : ℝ) * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) f := by ring
   177	  cases kind with
   178	  | axis =>
   179	      exact hcomponent (restrictedALineDist P.toLdParams) _
   180	        (aLinePointDist_eq_bind_restricted P.toLdParams) hAle
   181	  | diagonal =>
   182	      exact hcomponent (restrictedDLineDist P.toLdParams) _
   183	        (dLinePointDist_eq_bind_restricted P.toLdParams) hDle
   184	
   185	/-- Restricting a nonnegative average over two independent line-point samples
   186	to one kind and coordinate index in each factor inflates it by at most
   187	`4 m ^ 2`.  This is the pointwise form of item 2 of
   188	blueprint `lem:restricted-line-mixture-bounds`, paper
   189	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1056-1058`. -/
   190	theorem avgOver_prod_restrictedLinePointDist_le {P : AdmissibleParams}
   191	    (f : ((LineDesc P.toLdParams × (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)) ×
   192	      (LineDesc P.toLdParams × (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))) → ℝ)
   193	    (hf : ∀ sample, 0 ≤ f sample) (kindX kindZ : LineKind) (i j : Fin P.m) :
   194	    avgOver (Distribution.prod (restrictedLinePointDist P kindX i)
   195	        (restrictedLinePointDist P kindZ j)) f ≤
   196	      4 * (P.m : ℝ) ^ 2 * avgOver (Distribution.prod
   197	        (linePointDist P.toLdParams) (linePointDist P.toLdParams)) f := by
   198	  classical
   199	  have hfactor : (0 : ℝ) ≤ 2 * (P.m : ℝ) := by positivity
   200	  rw [avgOver_prod, avgOver_prod]
   201	  have hinner : ∀ s1 : LineDesc P.toLdParams × (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P),
   202	      avgOver (restrictedLinePointDist P kindZ j) (fun s2 => f (s1, s2)) ≤
   203	        2 * (P.m : ℝ) *
   204	          avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) (fun s2 => f (s1, s2)) :=
   205	    fun s1 => avgOver_restrictedLinePointDist_le
   206	      (fun s2 => f (s1, s2)) (fun s2 => hf (s1, s2)) kindZ j
   207	  calc avgOver (restrictedLinePointDist P kindX i)
   208	        (fun s1 => avgOver (restrictedLinePointDist P kindZ j)
   209	          (fun s2 => f (s1, s2)))
   210	      ≤ avgOver (restrictedLinePointDist P kindX i)
   211	          (fun s1 => 2 * (P.m : ℝ) *
   212	            avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams) (fun s2 => f (s1, s2))) :=
   213	        avgOver_mono _ _ _ hinner
   214	    _ = 2 * (P.m : ℝ) * avgOver (restrictedLinePointDist P kindX i)
   215	          (fun s1 => avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   216	            (fun s2 => f (s1, s2))) := avgOver_const_mul _ _ _
   217	    _ ≤ 2 * (P.m : ℝ) * (2 * (P.m : ℝ) *
   218	          avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   219	            (fun s1 => avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   220	              (fun s2 => f (s1, s2)))) := by
   221	        refine mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ?_ hfactor
   222	        exact avgOver_restrictedLinePointDist_le
   223	          (fun s1 => avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   224	            (fun s2 => f (s1, s2)))
   225	          (fun s1 => avgOver_nonneg _ _ fun s2 => hf (s1, s2)) kindX i
   226	    _ = 4 * (P.m : ℝ) ^ 2 * avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   227	          (fun s1 => avgOver (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   228	            (fun s2 => f (s1, s2))) := by ring
   229

    18	1038--1048.

     4	# Expanded line measurements
     5	
     6	For a generalized-Pauli basis `W` and a canonical line, the expanded line
     7	measurement is the convolution of the strategy line measurement with the
     8	projective measurement of one Pauli register whose outcome is the restriction
     9	to that line of the low-degree encoding of the measured basis label. This file
    10	states the three consistency conclusions the source draws for that family,
    11	together with the existential form in which the source states them.
    12	
    13	The argument runs as follows. Restricting a multilinear low-degree encoding to
    14	a line gives a polynomial of degree at most `m*d` in the line parameter, and at
    15	most `d` on an axis-parallel line (`LineMeasurement.Restriction`), whose
    16	partial evaluation at a sampled point obeys the elementary calculus of
    17	`LineMeasurement.Evaluation`.
    18	Coarse-graining the generalized Pauli basis measurement along that restriction
    19	gives the ancillary projectors `tau^{W,line}`, which are symmetric and hence
    20	perfectly self-consistent on an EPR pair (`LineMeasurement.Projector`). Their
    21	convolution with the strategy line measurement is again projective and vanishes
    22	outside the degree-`d` outcomes on an axis line (`LineMeasurement.Expanded`).
    23	Self-consistency of the convolution follows from self-consistency of the
    24	strategy line measurements and the data-processing inequality
    25	(`LineMeasurement.SelfConsistency`). The overlap of an expanded line
    26	measurement with the expanded point effects selected by evaluation at the
    27	sampled point factorizes exactly through the ancillary consistency of
    28	`tau^{W,line}` with `tau^{W,u}` (`LineMeasurement.LinePointOverlap`); the
    29	generic bipartite estimates of `LineMeasurement.BipartiteTransport` carry that
    30	overlap to the two bipartitions of the six registers, giving the
    31	evaluation-class conclusion (`LineMeasurement.EvalClassConsistency`) and, by
    32	projective refinement, the line-versus-point conclusion
    33	(`LineMeasurement.LinePointConsistency`).
    34	
    35	Two features of this route differ from the source. The source derives its third
    36	item from its second; here the evaluation-class estimate comes first, from the
    37	exact overlap identity, and the second item follows from it by projective
    38	refinement, so that the source's elementary sub-measurement inequality is not
    39	needed. The source also transports a relation proved for one pair of register
    40	placements to the remaining three by the symmetry of the test
    41	(`lem:symmetric-equivalents-transfer`, which is not formalized); here each of
    42	the four directed opposite-placement pairs is proved directly. The estimates
    43	established are linear in `ε` for all three items, hence stronger than the
    44	square-root error whenever `ε ≤ 1`; they are weakened to the common error
    45	`deltaLine ε = √ε` only because the source states the three items with a single
    46	error function (`LineMeasurement.SquareRootError`).

   802	\begin{lemma}[Combined point measurements]
   803		\label{lem:qld-4-10}
   804		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.CombinedPointsWitness}
   805		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_combinedPointsWitness}
   806		\leanok
   807		\uses{def:expanded-state, def:expanded-point-measurement,
   808			def:povm-distance, def:symmetric-equivalents}
   809		There exists a function $\delta_Q(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the
   810		following holds. For every $x, z \in \F_q^m$ and
   811		$\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ there are
   812		projective measurements $\{\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}\}_{a,b \in \F_q}$ acting
   813		on $\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot M}$ such that:
   814		\begin{enumerate}
   815			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random
   816			$x, z \in \F_q^m$,
   817			\begin{equation}
   818				\label{eq:qld-q-self-cons}
   819				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   820				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   821				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   822			\end{equation}
   823			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly
   824			random $x, z \in \F_q^m$,
   825			\begin{gather}
   826				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz}
   827				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   828				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   829				(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a} \,
   830				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,
   831				\\
   832				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}
   833				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   834				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   835				(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b} \,
   836				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   837			\end{gather}
   838		\end{enumerate}
   839		Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations also hold.
   840		The operators $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}$ and
   841		$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}$ do not commute in general, so the
   842		products in \eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz} and
   843		\eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx} differ and the two relations are separate
   844		conclusions.

   848		\uses{lem:qld-comm-cons, lem:ortho, fact:triangle,
   849			def:expanded-point-measurement, def:symmetric-equivalents,
   850			def:povm-distance}
   851		The formal proof works with field-valued outcomes directly. On each
   852		expanded local space form the complete sandwich POVM
   853		$R^{x,z}_{a,b}=M^{Z,z}_b M^{X,x}_a M^{Z,z}_b$.
   854		Field-valued approximate commutation bounds its distance from the ordered
   855		point product. Point self-consistency and the same commutation estimate
   856		bound its off-diagonal overlap across opposite placements.
   857		Apply orthonormalization to obtain a projective measurement for each
   858		point pair, on the same expanded local space, close to this POVM.

   874	\begin{lemma}[Formalization support for coefficient polynomial agreement]
   875		\label{lem:coefficient-polynomial-agreement}

+	Put $n=2m+2$. The directly indexed extended line-point law samples
+	$i\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $u,v\in\F_q^n$ independently and uniformly,
+	and chooses the axis or diagonal kind with equal probabilities.
+	For the axis kind set $w=e_i$; for the diagonal kind set $w_j=0$ for
+	$j<i$ and $w_j=v_j$ for $j\ge i$. The line has base $L_w^{\mathrm{lnf}}(u)$
+	and direction $w$, retaining its kind and coordinate index; the sampled
+	point is $u$. Zero diagonal directions are included.

+	A directly indexed sub-line law $D_{\mathrm{dir}}$ is a probability law
+	on triples $(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z)$ with the following properties.
+	Its extended-line marginal is the line marginal just defined.
+	Every supported triple admits affine maps $t\mapsto a_W+b_Wt$ such that
+	\[
+		\pi_W(\ell(t))=\ell_W(a_W+b_Wt),\qquad W\in\{X,Z\},
+	\]

+	field identifications are understood. Thus each extended point projects
+	onto its two source lines, with affine scalar coordinates $\alpha(t)$
+	and $\beta(t)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:combine-map}. An axis-parallel
+	extended line has axis-parallel source lines.

+	$(\mathrm v,i,j)\in\{\mathrm{ALine},\mathrm{DLine}\}
+	\times\{0,\dots,m-1\}^2$ with the following two mixture properties.
+	Sample a triple from $D_{\mathrm{dir}}$ and an independent uniform
+	parameter $t$ on $\ell$. The law of $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,\pi_X(\ell(t)))$
+	is the mixture obtained by sampling $(\ell_X,x)$ from
+	$D_{\mathrm v,i}$ and independently $\ell_Z$ from the line marginal of
+	$D_{\mathrm v,j}$, and retaining $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,x)$.
+	The law of $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,\pi_Z(\ell(t)))$ is the mixture obtained
+	by retaining $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,z)$ from the corresponding independent

+	$0\leq f(x,y)\leq C(x^r+y^s)$ on the closed nonnegative quadrant,

+	Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}.

   523	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:qld-comm-line-cons}
   524	There exists a function $\delta_{\Line}(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   525		For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and lines $\line$ there exists a projective measurement $\{ \hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f \}_{f \in \deg_{md}(\line)}$, acting on registers $\alice\alice'$ or $\bob\alice''$, such that:
   526		\begin{enumerate}
   527			\item  (\textbf{Self-consistency})\label{enu:qld-comm-line-self-cons}  For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $r \in \F_q$, on average over a uniformly random  pair $(\line, u)$
   528	                drawn from the line-point distribution
   529	                (\Cref{def:line-point-dist}),
   530			\[
   531				(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_\Line} (\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   532			\]
   533			
   534			\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements I}) \label{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons}
   535			On average over a uniformly random pair $(\line, u)$
   536	                drawn from the line-point distribution, 
   537			\[
   538				(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_\Line} (\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_{f(u)})_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   539			\]		
   540			\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements II}) \label{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons2}
   541			On average over a uniformly random pair $(\line, u)$
   542	                drawn from the line-point distribution,
   543			\[
   544				(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_{[\eval_u(\cdot) = a]})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_\Line}  (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_{a})_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   545			\]
   546	              \end{enumerate}
   547	                    Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations
   548	      also hold.
   549	\end{lemma}

    27	/-- Coordinates outside one low-degree register in the Pauli seed. -/
    28	abbrev PauliLdRemainder (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
    29	  (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) × PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P
    30	
    31	/-- Split a Pauli seed into a basis-selected low-degree seed and unused coordinates. -/
    32	private def pauliLdSplit (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind) :
    33	    PauliSpace P ≃ LdSpace P.toLdParams × PauliLdRemainder P where
    34	  toFun z :=
    35	    (pauliToLd P W z,
    36	      (match W with | .X => pauliZBlock z | .Z => pauliXBlock z,
    37	        pauliRXBlock z, pauliRZBlock z))
    38	  invFun zr := fun i =>
    39	    match i with
    40	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) =>
    41	        match W with
    42	        | .X => zr.1 (.inl (.inl j))
    43	        | .Z => zr.2.1 j
    44	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) =>
    45	        match W with
    46	        | .X => zr.2.1 j
    47	        | .Z => zr.1 (.inl (.inl j))
    48	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => zr.1 (.inl (.inr ()))
    49	    | .inl (.inl (.inr j)) => zr.1 (.inr j)
    50	    | .inl (.inr _) => zr.2.2.1
    51	    | .inr _ => zr.2.2.2
    52	  left_inv z := by
    53	    funext i
    54	    rcases i with ((((j | j) | u) | j) | u) | u <;> cases W <;> rfl
    55	  right_inv zr := by
    56	    rcases zr with ⟨z, other, rX, rZ⟩
    57	    apply Prod.ext
    58	    · funext i
    59	      rcases i with (j | u) | j <;> cases W <;> rfl
    60	    · cases W <;> rfl
    61	
    62	/-- Coordinates discarded by the shared Pair and Magic Square projection. -/
    63	abbrev PauliSharedRemainder (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
    64	  PauliScalar P × (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
    65	
    66	/-- Split a Pauli seed into its shared tuple and discarded scalar/direction blocks. -/
    67	def pauliSharedSplit (P : AdmissibleParams) :
    68	    PauliSpace P ≃ PauliTuple P × PauliSharedRemainder P where
    69	  toFun z :=
    70	    ((pauliXBlock z, pauliZBlock z, pauliRXBlock z, pauliRZBlock z),
    71	      pauliScalarBlock z, pauliDirectionBlock z)
    72	  invFun zr := fun i =>
    73	    match i with
    74	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) => zr.1.1 j
    75	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) => zr.1.2.1 j
    76	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => zr.2.1
    77	    | .inl (.inl (.inr j)) => zr.2.2 j
    78	    | .inl (.inr _) => zr.1.2.2.1
    79	    | .inr _ => zr.1.2.2.2
    80	  left_inv z := by
    81	    funext i
    82	    rcases i with ((((j | j) | u) | j) | u) | u <;> rfl
    83	  right_inv zr := by
    84	    rcases zr with ⟨⟨uX, uZ, rX, rZ⟩, scalar, direction⟩
    85	    rfl

1	# Mathematical Language Guidelines
     2	
     3	MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
     4	the formalization with the paper and blueprint.
     5	
     6	This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
     7	naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
     8	`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.
     9	
    10	## Scope
    11	
    12	These guidelines apply to:
    13	
    14	- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
    15	- module docstrings;
    16	- declaration docstrings;
    17	- documentation-visible section comments;
    18	- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
    19	- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
    20	- issue titles and issue bodies;
    21	- PR titles and PR descriptions.
    22	
    23	## Source of Truth
    24	
    25	Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:
    26	
    27	1. `references/ldt-paper/`
    28	2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
    29	3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files
    30	
    31	When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
    32	example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
    33	projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.
    34	
    35	## Reference Notation And Terminology
    36	
    37	The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
    38	reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
    39	docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
    40	without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.
    41	
    42	When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
    43	location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
    44	first applicable location in the following order:
    45	
    46	1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
    47	   differs from the paper;
    48	2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
    49	   family of declarations in that file;
    50	3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
    51	   blueprint;
    52	4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
    53	   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.
    54	
    55	The explanation should say:
    56	
    57	- the notation or term used in the paper;
    58	- the Lean object or name which represents it;
    59	- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.
    86	
    87	### Concrete examples
    88	
    89	The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
    90	codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
    91	others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
    92	process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
    93	assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
    94	paper or blueprint would recognize.
    95	
    96	| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
    97	|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
    98	| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
    99	| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
   100	| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
   101	| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
   102	| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
   103	| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
   104	| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
   105	| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
   106	| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
   107	| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |
   108	
   109	An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
   110	phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
   111	In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.
   112	
   113	File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
   114	named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
   115	exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.
   116	
   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124

   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,

   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or

   147	/-- For a positive operator `A`, the sesquilinear form `⟨u, A v⟩` satisfies the

   149	`⟨v, A v⟩`.  This is the inequality behind the Cauchy--Schwarz steps of the
   150	proofs of `lem:claim-17-2` and `lem:claim-17-3`, in which both factors carry

   154	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {A : Op ι} (hA : 0 ≤ A)

   156	    ‖inner ℂ u (applyOperatorToState A v)‖ ≤
   157	      Real.sqrt (inner ℂ u (applyOperatorToState A u)).re *
   158	        Real.sqrt (inner ℂ v (applyOperatorToState A v)).re := by

   161	  have hRR : R * R = A := CFC.sqrt_mul_sqrt_self A hA
   162	  have hRherm : Rᴴ = R :=
   163	    (Matrix.nonneg_iff_posSemidef.mp hRnonneg).isHermitian.eq
   164	  have hadjoint : (Matrix.toEuclideanLin R).adjoint = Matrix.toEuclideanLin R := by

   169	    intro w z
   170	    have h := LinearMap.adjoint_inner_right (Matrix.toEuclideanLin R) w
   171	      (Matrix.toEuclideanLin R z)
   172	    rw [hadjoint] at h
   173	    rw [← hRR, applyOperatorToState_mul]
   174	    exact h

     8	2. **Standalone.** `blueprint/` and any slides are independent — no cross-references, no shared files. Each has its own macros, its own `references.bib`.
     9	3. **Mathematical language only — zero Lean jargon.** No Lean identifiers in prose (no `selfImprovement_step`, no `PastingLemma.aux`, no `rintro ⟨X, hX⟩`). The `\lean{...}` tag is the link; the body text is standard mathematics. If you can't say it in math, rewrite it.
    10	4. **No filler prose.** Only precise definitions, theorem statements, and proof sketches. No "this is important because..." or "the self-improvement step governs the induction...".
    11	5. **Cite non-trivial things.** Basic definitions don't need citations. Important results and non-obvious definitions should cite the source paper.
    12	6. **Don't invent terminology or notation.** Don't create ad-hoc notation when standard notation exists. Don't name things that the literature doesn't name.
    13	7. **Match Lean's theorem/lemma/def exactly.** If Lean says `theorem X`, use `\begin{theorem}`. If Lean says `lemma X`, use `\begin{lemma}`. `\begin{proposition}` is allowed in blueprint prose when it improves mathematical readability, but still map it to an actual Lean `theorem`/`lemma` declaration via `\lean{...}`. Label prefix: `thm:` for theorem, `lem:` for lemma, `def:` for definition, `prop:` for proposition.
    14	
    15	### Remark On Mathematical Prose
    16	
    17	Blueprint entries should read as mathematical exposition, not as progress
    18	reports. The mathematical argument should determine the order of the prose:
    19	introduce the notation, state the assertion, give the proof or calculation, and
    20	then record Lean references through the usual blueprint tags. Lean declarations,
    21	file paths, and proof-status information should not become the visible structure
    22	of the paragraph. When referring to a source article, cite it bibliographically
    23	rather than relying on an uncited reference to the article.
    24	
    25	Use displayed formulae when the formula benefits from visual separation, and
    26	keep short scalar definitions or elementary inequalities inline when the
    27	sentence reads better that way. As in ordinary mathematical writing, displayed
    28	formulae should be punctuated as part of the sentences in which they occur.
    29	
    30	## Proof Sketches Must Match Lean
    31	This is the most important rule. Every proof in the blueprint must faithfully describe what the Lean proof does:
    32	
    33	- **Reference the actual lemmas used.** If the Lean proof calls `LDT.selfImprovement`, the blueprint proof should say "By Lemma X.Y (self-improvement)..." and list it in `\uses`.
    34	- **Do not use `\cref` or `\Cref`.** The blueprint does not load `cleveref`.
    35	  Spell out the kind of object and use ordinary references, for example
    36	  `Lemma~\ref{lem:self-improvement}` or `Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}`.
    37	- **Describe the actual proof structure.** If Lean does induction on a parameter, say so. If Lean uses a specific decomposition, name it.
    38	- **Don't hand-wave where Lean is specific.** "Standard argument" is not acceptable if Lean uses three specific lemmas. Name them.
    39	- **Don't be more specific than Lean.** If Lean uses `simp` to close a goal, a one-line sketch is fine.
    40	- **`\uses` in proofs must be accurate.** Only list what the proof actually uses, not what the statement mentions.
    41	
    42	## Source-Labelled Statements And Conditional Helpers
    43	
    44	If a blueprint theorem, lemma, or proposition carries a source label from the
    45	paper, the linked Lean declaration must state the same theorem, up to faithful
    46	formal encoding of the paper's domain.  Do not use `\lean{...}` and `\leanok`
    47	on the source-labelled statement to point to a conditional helper whose
    48	additional assumptions supply an unproved part of the paper proof.
    49	Changing the Lean statement away from `references/ldt-paper/` is strongly
    50	discouraged unless faithful formal encoding or a documented mathematical
    51	necessity requires it; the blueprint should make any such necessity explicit.
    52	
    53	Boundary hypotheses such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
    54	positivity of parameters, and denominator nonvanishing may be faithful when
    55	they express the mathematical domain that the paper leaves implicit.  By
    56	contrast, bridge inputs, residual data, repair hypotheses, producer
    57	assumptions, proof-obligation inputs, or package assumptions are proof debt.
    58	They must not be added to a source-labelled theorem statement.  If such data is
    59	still unproved, the source-labelled Lean theorem should keep the source-shaped
    60	statement and carry a tracked `sorry`, or the missing assertion should appear
    61	as the lowest named internal obligation with a tracked `sorry`.  A separately
    62	named conditional helper should not be introduced as a repair pattern.  If one
    63	already contains substantial proof content, it may remain temporarily only as
    64	quarantine: it needs a paper source, a tracking issue, and a discharge or
    65	deletion plan.  The blueprint should leave the paper theorem unmarked as
    66	proof-complete until the source-faithful Lean statement has a source-faithful
    67	proof.
    68	
    69	If a Lean theorem proves only a restricted version of a source theorem, the
    70	blueprint entry carrying `\leanok` must state that restriction in the theorem
    71	statement itself.  It must not be cited as the unrestricted source theorem.
    72	When the only Lean declaration available for a source label has extra
    73	non-paper assumptions, remove the `\leanok` claim from the source-labelled
    74	entry or move the restricted statement to a separate Lean-only entry.  The
    75	unrestricted paper theorem remains unformalized until a Lean statement with
    76	the source's hypothesis set exists.
    77	
    78	## Notation Consistency
    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:
    80	
    81	- **Indices**: 0-indexed where matching `Fin n` in Lean
    82	- **Finite fields / alphabets**: use standard notation for the alphabet $\Sigma$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
    83	- **Measurements**: use standard quantum measurement notation (projective measurements, POVMs)
    84	- **Strategies**: quantum strategies for nonlocal games should use standard notation from the literature
    85	- **Expansion**: use standard notation for graph expansion parameters
    86	- **Macros** (in `macros/common.tex`): define project-specific macros and use them consistently
    87	
    88	The original reference controls notation whenever it gives a usable convention.
    89	If the blueprint needs a different symbol, index convention, or name in order to
    90	match Lean, introduce it explicitly and relate it to the paper notation in the
    91	same paragraph.  Do not let a `\lean{...}` tag, a Lean namespace, or a file name
    92	be the only explanation of a changed term.
    93	
    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the
    95	blueprint should say so before listing the declaration.  The surrounding prose
    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary
    97	lemma supports, and should avoid making the auxiliary name look like a named
    98	result from the source article.
    99	
   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.
   135	
   136	## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  anchored paper passage, or blueprint label it supports. Blueprint line
   147	  ranges are derived review context, not stored docstring citations; resolve a
   148	  label with `python3 scripts/blueprint_citations.py resolve <label>`.
   149	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   150	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   151	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   152	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
   153	  Lean proof.
   154	- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
   155	  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
   156	  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
   157	  used.
   158	- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
   159	  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
   160	  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
   161	  proof remains tracked as incomplete.
   162	
   163	## Blueprint Structure
   164	- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
   165	- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
   166	- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`
   167	
   168	## Lean Blueprint Macros
   169	- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
   170	- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
   171	- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
   172	- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
   173	- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)
   174	
   175	### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`
   176	
   177	`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.
   178	
   179	**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
relevant audit before changing names or prose.

+\begin{definition}[Directly indexed sub-line laws]

+	\uses{def:ith-restricted-line, def:line-representative, def:combine-map}
+	Put $n=2m+2$. The directly indexed extended line-point law samples
+	$i\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $u,v\in\F_q^n$ independently and uniformly,
+	and chooses the axis or diagonal kind with equal probabilities.
+	For the axis kind set $w=e_i$; for the diagonal kind set $w_j=0$ for
+	$j<i$ and $w_j=v_j$ for $j\ge i$. The line has base $L_w^{\mathrm{lnf}}(u)$
+	and direction $w$, retaining its kind and coordinate index; the sampled
+	point is $u$. Zero diagonal directions are included.
+
+	A directly indexed sub-line law $D_{\mathrm{dir}}$ is a probability law
+	on triples $(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z)$ with the following properties.
+	Its extended-line marginal is the line marginal just defined.
+	Every supported triple admits affine maps $t\mapsto a_W+b_Wt$ such that
+	\[
+		\pi_W(\ell(t))=\ell_W(a_W+b_Wt),\qquad W\in\{X,Z\},

+	field identifications are understood. Thus each extended point projects
+	onto its two source lines, with affine scalar coordinates $\alpha(t)$
+	and $\beta(t)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:combine-map}. An axis-parallel
+	extended line has axis-parallel source lines.
+
+	Finally there is one probability law on
+	$(\mathrm v,i,j)\in\{\mathrm{ALine},\mathrm{DLine}\}
+	\times\{0,\dots,m-1\}^2$ with the following two mixture properties.
+	Sample a triple from $D_{\mathrm{dir}}$ and an independent uniform
+	parameter $t$ on $\ell$. The law of $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,\pi_X(\ell(t)))$
+	is the mixture obtained by sampling $(\ell_X,x)$ from
+	$D_{\mathrm v,i}$ and independently $\ell_Z$ from the line marginal of
+	$D_{\mathrm v,j}$, and retaining $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,x)$.
+	The law of $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,\pi_Z(\ell(t)))$ is the mixture obtained
+	by retaining $(\ell_X,\ell_Z,z)$ from the corresponding independent
+	samples of $\ell_X$ and $(\ell_Z,z)$. These are separate one-point
+	marginal identities, with the same mixture weights; they impose no
+	joint conditional independence of the two projected points.
+	Identification with the source law $D$ is a separate obligation;
+	see \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}.
